item.title: Distributed Neural Dynamics Underlie the Shift from Movement Preparation to Execution.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Understanding how neural population activity supports the transition from movement preparation to execution remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience. Invasive recordings in nonhuman primates indicate that motor preparation and execution occupy orthogonal subspaces within the primary motor cortex (M1), yet how these neural dynamics evolve across broader networks and support skilled, memory-guided action remains poorly understood. We used source-resolved magnetoencephalography during a memory-guided finger-sequence task to track population dynamics across a cortico-hippocampal network. Manifold trajectories and decoding revealed that preparation and execution of movement sequences occupy distinct, yet not fully orthogonal, neural subspaces-a separation that generalized across all regions but was most pronounced in motor regions. Crucially, we identified a hierarchical spatio-temporal transition across the brain: The state shift originated in the hippocampus via theta-band modulations and rippled through the pre-SMA, SMA, and lateral premotor areas before culminating in M1 via broadband activity. This progression follows the functional hierarchy of descending motor pathways, with M1 shifting last, 160 msec before the first button press. Although sequence identity could be decoded from all areas during execution, only the hippocampus and M1 maintained predictive representations of upcoming sequences during preparation. These findings demonstrate that the initiation of complex motor sequences relies on a well-timed integration of hippocampal memory systems with primary motor output, rather than being a process localized to the motor cortices alone.

item.title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low-trust Speakers.
item.description:
Journal of cognitive neuroscience
Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using noninvasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from 20 young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal temporal response function dynamics.

item.title: Evaluation of Brain Activity in Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder Using Standardized Low Resolution Electromagnetic Tomographic Analyses (sLORETA).
item.description:
Clinical EEG and neuroscience
This study evaluated Default Mode Network (DMN) brain activity in females with Premenstrual Dysphoric Disorder (PMDD)/Dysphoric PMS and asymptomatic controls using archival quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG) and standardized low-resolution brain electromagnetic tomography (sLORETA) data. Eyes-closed resting-state EEG analyses were examined across follicular and luteal menstrual cycle phases. The analytic sample included 157 participants: PMDD/Dysphoric PMS (n = 87) and asymptomatic controls (n = 70). Nonparametric Wilcoxon Signed Rank Tests were used for follicular-to-luteal within-group comparisons, and Mood's Median Test was used for luteal-phase between-group analyses. Asymptomatic controls showed significant follicular-to-luteal mean-Z changes in cingulate gyrus delta, cingulate gyrus theta, and insula theta. PMDD/Dysphoric PMS participants showed a significant percentage-of-aberrant-voxels change in angular gyrus beta2. During the luteal phase, PMDD/Dysphoric PMS participants showed significantly higher subcallosal-gyrus beta2 mean-Z activity than asymptomatic controls. Luteal subcallosal-gyrus beta2 abnormal-voxel values were descriptively higher in PMDD/Dysphoric PMS participants (19.43%) than in asymptomatic controls (4.13%); however, this voxel-percentage comparison is reported descriptively because luteal-phase between-group percentage-of-voxels analyses did not reach the study threshold for statistical significance. These findings support further investigation of DMN-linked neural activity, subcallosal-gyrus beta2 activity, and phase-related network adaptability in PMDD.

item.title: From sensorimotor to transmodal cortex: sleep quality aligns brain entropy with the cortical functional gradient.
item.description:
Sleep
STUDY OBJECTIVES: Sleep is fundamental to brain health, yet the mechanisms by which habitual sleep quality shapes large-scale neural dynamics during wakefulness remain unclear. This work aims at determining whether habitual sleep quality is associated with systematic alterations in regional and cross-regional temporal complexity of spontaneous neural activity. METHODS: Regional brain entropy (BEN) and cross-regional brain entropy were estimated from resting-state fMRI data of the UK Biobank, with replication in the Human Connectome Project and in a randomized total sleep deprivation experiment. Temporal complexity of spontaneous neural activity was correlated to self-reported habitual sleep quality and sleep amount in observational cohorts and experimental total sleep deprivation in the laboratory study. RESULTS: Better sleep quality was associated with increased BEN in sensory and sensorimotor cortices and decreased BEN in frontoparietal control regions. High-quality sleep enhanced differentiation of temporal complexity among sensory networks while strengthening coordination within higher-order control systems. In the independent Human Connectome Project cohort, sleep amount predicted increased BEN in visual and somatomotor regions. Moreover, the strength of the association between sleep measures and BEN was strongly and negatively correlated with the major cortical functional gradient. Exploratory results suggest convergent effects following total sleep deprivation. Habitual sleep quality is associated with systematic reconfiguration of the brain's temporal complexity architecture at both regional and network levels. CONCLUSION: These findings position sleep as a fundamental determinant of the brain's dynamic operating regime and identify temporal complexity as a mechanistically informative neural signature linking sleep health to cognitive function and neuropsychiatric vulnerability.

item.title: Vitamin B12 deficiency, cerebral myelination, and language development: biological evidence from an integrative review.
item.description:
Developmental neurorehabilitation
OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to analyze scientific evidence on the relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency, cerebral myelination, and its potential implications for language development and speech fluency. METHODS: An integrative literature review was conducted using the PubMed, Scopus, and Cochrane databases between August 2025 and July 2026. The search strategy included terms related to vitamin B12, myelination, brain development, language, and speech. Original studies published in English investigating the effects of vitamin B12 deficiency on the central nervous system, neurodevelopment, or structural brain changes were included. RESULTS: Thirteen studies met the eligibility criteria and were synthesized through thematic narrative analysis. The findings indicated a relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency and delayed neuropsychomotor development, impaired myelination, reduced white matter integrity, and structural brain abnormalities identified by neuroimaging. Furthermore, studies investigating the neural circuits underlying language showed that these same structures are essential for language organization and speech fluency, providing biological plausibility for a potential relationship between vitamin B12 deficiency and impairments in these processes. CONCLUSION: Vitamin B12 deficiency may adversely affect neurodevelopment and cerebral myelination, representing a potential mechanism underlying alterations in the maturation of neural circuits involved in language. These findings support the biological plausibility that vitamin B12 deficiency may contribute to impaired language development through disrupted cerebral myelination, although direct clinical evidence remains lacking.

item.title: The unfolding symphony: unraveling brain dynamics via data-driven multi-scale functional connectivity in task-state fMRI.
item.description:
Brain structure & function
Task-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) can characterize both regional responses and changes in statistical dependence among distributed brain systems. This narrative review examines dynamic and multiscale connectivity within a broader framework that distinguishes task-modulated functional connectivity, trial-wise covariation, effective connectivity, and data-driven state analysis. Sliding-window correlation, hidden Markov models, and co-activation patterns are compared by their data representations, temporal assumptions, and computational procedures; graph representations can be combined with each of these strategies. We discuss supervised recurrent, transformer, and graph models alongside unsupervised state discovery, self-supervised representation learning, and emerging brain foundation models. Explainability requires evaluation of model attributions, including graph masks and perturbation-based analyses, rather than anatomical plausibility alone. The spatial framework includes whole-brain networks, subnetworks, atlas-defined regions of interest, and voxel- or layer-level measurements. Proposed links across these levels remain hypotheses: faster sampling of the blood oxygenation level-dependent (BOLD) signal does not directly resolve millisecond neural interactions, and resting-state or animal findings do not establish the corresponding mechanism during human tasks. Shared task-evoked responses, hemodynamic variability, motion, and analytical choices can all alter apparent connectivity. Progress therefore depends on matching the estimator to the scientific question, comparing against activation and static-connectivity baselines, and validating results across participants, sessions, and acquisition settings.

item.title: Subliminal beauty engages the brain's valuation circuits.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
Neuroeconomic models propose that the anterior ventral striatum (aVS) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) are key regions for computing subjective value (SV) signals that guide choice. However, the role of conscious awareness in this process remains debated. Here we examined whether SV can be automatically computed in these regions without conscious awareness. In an fMRI experiment, human participants (24 females, 5 males) viewed faces that varied in attractiveness under three conditions: (i) suppressed from awareness via continuous flash suppression (CFS), (ii) clearly visible without suppression, or (iii) absent (background only) with CFS. Participants reported trial-wise facial identity (objective) and visibility (subjective) measures of facial awareness. In a post-fMRI session, they rated the attractiveness of each face as a measure of SV. When faces were seen, task performance (d') exceeded chance and responses were faster than in absent trials. When faces were unseen, performance was at chance but responses were slower than absent trials. Neurally, seen and unseen faces elicited greater neural signal than absent trials and showed similar neural patterns in the fusiform face area (FFA). Critically, neural signal in vmPFC correlated with SV for both seen and unseen faces, with similar neural patterns. In aVS, SV-related signal was only observed for unseen faces. Furthermore, mean face-related signal in FFA correlated with SV-related signals in aVS and vmPFC for unseen faces. These findings demonstrate that SV can be automatically computed in aVS and vmPFC without conscious awareness, suggesting a neural pathway by which subliminal information can influence value-based choice.Significance statement A central question in consciousness research and decision neuroscience is whether the brain's valuation circuitry - particularly the anterior ventral striatum (aVS) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) - can compute subjective value automatically without conscious awareness. This question is important because prevailing accounts often assume that cognitive functions supported by the prefrontal cortex require conscious awareness of task-relevant information. Using continuous flash suppression and neuroimaging, we found that faces reported unseen nevertheless evoked value-related signals in aVS and vmPFC that scaled with subjective attractiveness ratings. These findings demonstrate that subjective value can be computed automatically from social information in the absence of conscious awareness.

item.title: During natural vision, semantic novelty modulates fixation-related processing in primate cortex.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
We sample visual scenes with short gaze fixations separated by saccades. While low-level integration is known, semantic integration of foveal vision across fixations remains unclear. We hypothesized that the brain responds to changes in semantic information from one fixation to the next, and therefore postulated a neural signal associated with semantic novelty for each saccade. Novelty was measured from different layers of a deep network on foveal vision. Only semantic, and not low- or mid-level, novelty modulated frontal and occipital fixation-related potentials in male and female human scalp EEG during natural viewing of full-length movies (3.4x106 saccades). Intracranial recordings in male and female humans (9.0x104 saccades) and female non-human primates (Macaca mulatta; 3.3x104 saccades) revealed broadband high-frequency activity modulations in scene-specific ventral visual and frontal brain areas only for semantic novelty. This modulation was stronger for movies than static images, and frontal modulation occurred early alongside occipital modulation, suggesting top-down effects. This modulation of fixation-related activity with novelty suggests that foveal representations are compared between consecutive fixations to construct scene representations during natural viewing in primates.Significance statement Primate vision relies on eye movements to sample the world, yet how the brain integrates high-level meaning across these "snapshots" remains a mystery. By combining deep-learning models with massive electrophysiological datasets from humans and macaques, we show that the brain responds to changes in semantic content between fixations, but not low- or mid-level changes. We identified a "semantic novelty" signal that modulates neural activity across the primate cortex. These findings suggest visual processing is not a series of independent glimpses, but a continuous process comparing consecutive foveal information at the semantic level. This work bridges biological vision and artificial intelligence, providing a new framework for understanding how the brain maintains a coherent understanding of a dynamic world.

item.title: Beyond the cortex, early deficits, late recovery: a systematic review of language outcomes and subcortical mapping after awake craniotomy for diffuse gliomas.
item.description:
Chinese neurosurgical journal
BACKGROUND: To evaluate immediate and long-term postoperative language outcomes in patients undergoing awake craniotomy with direct electrical stimulation (DES) for diffuse gliomas in eloquent regions. METHODS: PRISMA-compliant systematic review (PROSPERO: CRD420261342690) of adults (≥ 18 years) with supratentorial diffuse glioma in the language-dominant hemisphere enrolled in both randomised and non-randomised studies of awake craniotomy with direct electrical stimulation and language mapping. Databases searched included PubMed, MEDLINE, Embase, and Cochrane CENTRAL (from 2010 to March 2026). Study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by multiple reviewers using standardised tools (JBI Critical Appraisal Checklists). Due to methodological heterogeneity, narrative synthesis was performed. RESULTS: Ten studies (532 patients enrolled; 55.3% male) published 2011-2025 were included; tumour grade was reported inconsistently, with higher-grade tumours predominating in the larger cohorts and at least 114 patients having WHO grade 4 disease. Early postoperative deficits ranged from 2.2 to 100% depending on assessment timing and measure (immediate post-op: up to 100%; day 7 to week 1: 2.2-22%). Persistent deficits at ≥ 3 months ranged from 0 to 47%. In three studies reporting whole-cohort outcomes with standardised assessment, rates were 0-5.6%. Papagno et al., using 3-month cut-offs, found that 47% of patients with uncinate fasciculus resection had impairment in famous face naming versus 10% with the tract preserved. The general trend was early decline followed by improvement, with most reported deficits resolving by around 3 months. Heterogeneous deficit definitions and inconsistent baseline assessment preclude treating this as a prognostic pattern, and resections involving the uncinate fasciculus were a notable outlier, underscoring the need for systematic subcortical tract mapping. CONCLUSION: Awake craniotomy with DES remains the gold standard for preserving language. Early deficits are common but predominantly transient, and reported deficit rates appear closely associated with the timing of assessment. Persistent deficits assessed at ≥ 3 months were low in most studies, although rates varied considerably with the outcome measure used and with subcortical tract involvement. Subcortical tract involvement warrants systematic mapping. We advocate for the global adoption of standardised perioperative linguistic protocols to improve data comparability. SYSTEMATIC REVIEW REGISTRATION: PROSPERO CRD420261342690.

item.title: Functional brain connectivity in patients with anorexia nervosa before and after short-term weight restoration.
item.description:
Journal of child psychology and psychiatry, and allied disciplines
BACKGROUND: Resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) studies have consistently identified widespread alterations in the brain's functional network architecture in anorexia nervosa (AN), but it remains unclear whether they are reversible with weight restoration. Furthermore, it is not clear whether there are associations between RSFC and neuroendocrine changes, such as leptin suppression in the underweight state of AN and its increase during short-term weight restoration. METHODS: We first analyzed RSFC data cross-sectionally in young female patients with AN (n = 117) and healthy control participants (n = 117) using network-based statistic (NBS) and graph theory metrics and subsequently explored relationships with plasma leptin as a marker of undernutrition. A subset of patients (n = 73) was reassessed longitudinally after short-term weight restoration [mean body mass index (BMI) increase: 28.0%] to test for changes in identified alterations. RESULTS: NBS revealed increased RSFC in cingulo-occipito-cerebellar circuitry in underweight patients with AN (p = .0018), which decreased over the inpatient weight restoration interval (p < .001). This change correlated negatively with plasma leptin concentrations (p = .042), and plasma leptin appeared to partially mediate the association between BMI increase and RSFC decrease (p = .039), suggesting a possible region-specific modulatory effect. Underweight patients with AN also showed higher characteristic path length (p = .035), indicating reduced integration between brain regions, and higher assortativity (p = .013), indicating stronger coupling among similarly connected regions. Longitudinally, characteristic path length decreased during weight restoration (p = .004), whereas findings for assortativity were suggestive of no change. CONCLUSIONS: The results provide novel longitudinal evidence that functional connectome alterations in AN partially normalize during short-term weight restoration. Speculatively, taking previous results in long-term recovered individuals into consideration, higher assortativity might reflect potential vulnerability for AN. Our finding of a tentative association between the normalization of plasma leptin concentrations and RSFC suggests the possibility that leptin may modulate changes in specific patterns of functional connectivity, offering a potential neurobiological target for novel pharmacotherapies.

item.title: Structural changes in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex following a randomized clinical trial of virtual reality-based cognitive remediation in mood and schizophrenia spectrum disorders.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
INTRODUCTION: Cognitive impairments are common in patients with mood disorders (MD) and schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD) and impair quality of life. Developing pro-cognitive treatments is hindered by limited understanding of the biology underlying cognitive impairment and improvement. This structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) study examined the neural correlates of cognitive improvement following a Virtual-Reality-based Cognitive Remediation Therapy (VR-CRT) intervention. METHODS: Patients underwent eight VR-CRT or VR-control treatment sessions during a four-week period. The study population included data from a transdiagnostic subsample of 41 symptomatically stable, cognitively impaired patients with MD or SSD (VR-CRT: n = 22; VR-control: n = 19) with baseline structural MRI data of which 33 (VR-CRT: 20; VR-control: n = 13) also underwent MRI at treatment completion. Neuropsychological assessment was completed both pre- and post-treatment and additionally at three-month post-treatment follow-up. RESULTS: Gray matter volume in the VR-CRT group increased over time in the right caudal middle frontal gyrus (MFG) compared to VR-control. Secondary hypothesis-driven analysis showed a similar increase in right caudal MFG thickness for VR-CRT patients. These structural changes were not associated with treatment-related cognitive improvement. However, greater left rostral MFG thickness at baseline was associated with more cognitive improvement over time in the VR-CRT group. CONCLUSION: This study demonstrates treatment-related structural changes in the right caudal MFG and suggests that baseline left rostral MFG thickness may represent a candidate marker of cognitive improvement within the VR-CRT group. These findings support further investigation of MFG structure as a marker of brain response and cognitive treatment outcome. This trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT06038955, and is completed.

item.title: Differential structural profiles of the hippocampus and thalamus and their cognitive relevance in unilateral mesial temporal lobe epilepsy.
item.description:
Progress in neuro-psychopharmacology & biological psychiatry
BACKGROUND: Cognitive dysfunction is common in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE), yet how much the hippocampus and the thalamus each contribute remains unclear. We compared fine-grained hippocampal and thalamic structure and their cognitive relevance in unilateral MTLE. METHODS: We studied 71 patients with unilateral MTLE (39 with hippocampal sclerosis [HS], 32 without) and 17 controls. FreeSurfer-derived cortical, hippocampal-subfield, and thalamic-nucleus volumes were compared using permutation-based general linear models. In patients, 19 cognitive measures were related to volume using covariate-adjusted partial correlations under seizure-referenced (ipsilateral/contralateral) and anatomical left/right codings. Nested additive models tested the incremental cognitive contributions of hippocampal and thalamic volume. RESULTS: Relative to controls, patients showed widespread thalamic atrophy (34 of 44 nuclei in the full cohort, 32 of 44 in each subgroup), whereas hippocampal subfield atrophy was largely confined to HS and no cortical region survived correction. All 48 corrected volume-cognition associations involved hippocampal subfields; none involved thalamic nuclei. Additive models showed that ipsilateral hippocampal volume explained 7.4%-14.6% of cognitive variance alone and explained an additional 6.8%-18.9% of cognitive variance beyond thalamic volume, whereas global thalamic volume did not add significant corrected incremental variance. Preserving anatomical hemisphere linked verbal comprehension and naming to left hippocampal subfields and working memory predominantly to right subfields. CONCLUSIONS: Hippocampal and thalamic abnormalities showed distinct structural and cognitive profiles in unilateral MTLE. Thalamic atrophy was widespread, whereas hippocampal volume was more closely related to cognition and showed additional variation by HS status and anatomical hemisphere.

item.title: Regional cortical thinning in cerebral small vessel disease: associations with disease burden and cognitive and motor impairment.
item.description:
Neuroscience
Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) is a major cause of cognitive decline and mobility impairment, yet whether cortical thickness and cortical volume provide similar or complementary information across different levels of CSVD burden remains unclear. We examined regional cortical thickness and cortical volume in healthy controls and participants with CSVD using high-resolution structural magnetic resonance imaging and FreeSurfer-based parcellation. Greater CSVD burden was associated with thinning across bilateral insular, occipital, temporal, cingulate, and cuneal regions, whereas cortical volume alterations were more spatially restricted, with only the left parahippocampal gyrus surviving Bonferroni correction. After adjustment for demographic characteristics, vascular risk factors, apolipoprotein E genotype, and mean cortical thickness, associations remained evident in the bilateral insulae and selected occipital and temporal regions. Regional cortical thickness was also related to cognitive and mobility performance. Exploratory incremental analyses showed that regional cortical thickness remained associated with cognitive performance in several regions after accounting for the corresponding regional cortical volume, intracranial volume, and other covariates. These findings suggest that cortical thickness and cortical volume may capture partly distinct aspects of cortical morphology in CSVD, with cortical thickness potentially providing complementary information related to cognitive performance.

item.title: Broadband gamma-band EEG changes during magnetophosphene-inducing 20 Hz magnetic field stimulation.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Magnetophosphenes are visual percepts induced by extremely low-frequency magnetic fields (ELF-MF; <300 Hz), yet the EEG expression of suprathreshold magnetophosphene-inducing stimulation remains poorly characterized and is not reliably captured by classical low-frequency markers. We tested whether suprathreshold 20 Hz tAMS is accompanied by broadband high-frequency EEG changes rather than focal oscillatory effects. EEG was recorded in N=13 healthy volunteers during 20 Hz sinusoidal magnetic-field exposure delivered using transcranial alternating magnetic stimulation (tAMS) in a global-head configuration. Three conditions were analyzed: no exposure (0 mT), subthreshold (5 mT), and suprathreshold (50 mT). Gamma-band EEG power (30-80 Hz) was quantified using complementary spectral approaches, including aperiodic-adjusted gamma power. Perception reports sharply dissociated the three conditions, with frequent perception at 50 mT only. Suprathreshold stimulation was associated with spatially distributed increases in gamma-band EEG power over frontal and occipito-parietal electrodes. The differences remained partly detectable in complementary analyses using two local aperiodic-adjustment methods and did not exhibit a consistent narrowband peak, a pattern consistent with broadband high-frequency changes. No focal power change over primary occipital electrodes remained significant after Bonferroni correction. These findings identify a spatially distributed broadband high-frequency scalp EEG effect associated with the suprathreshold 50 mT condition, with the main spatial pattern strongly preserved after ICA-based removal of components classified as ocular or muscular. The effect therefore characterizes the coupled suprathreshold stimulation-perception condition; its perception specificity and physiological source remain unresolved.

item.title: Glycemic control is differentially related to spontaneous cortical activity in patients on the Alzheimer's disease spectrum.
item.description:
GeroScience
Diabetes is a major risk factor for developing cognitive impairment and studies have shown that poor glycemic control can increase this risk, but the neural mechanisms are poorly understood. Many studies have linked altered spontaneous cortical activity during the resting-state to Alzheimer's disease and other neurological conditions associated with cognitive impairment. Herein, we examine whether the strength of spontaneous activity during the resting-state is differentially related to glycemic control in 37 biomarker-positive participants on the Alzheimer's disease spectrum (ADS) and 43 cognitively normal aging adults. All participants completed resting-state magnetoencephalography (MEG), a blood draw to derive their level of glycemic control (i.e., A1C), and comprehensive neuropsychological assessment. Spontaneous activity was imaged in each of the canonical frequency bands (e.g., alpha) and probed for group differences in the relationship between neural activity and glycemic control. We found significant interactions between A1C and disease status (ADS vs. control) in the delta and alpha bands (p < 0.001). Specifically, delta power decreased with increasing A1C in the ADS group across a broad area of frontotemporal and inferior parietal cortices, while spontaneous alpha decreased with higher A1C in the control group across inferior frontal and temporal cortex. Importantly, delta activity in the superior frontal cortices mediated the effect of A1C on attention performance in the ADS group. In sum, these data suggest that the impact of glycemic dysregulation on spontaneous cortical activity may differ in those on the ADS compared with cognitively normal controls and that spontaneous delta may be critical for attention function.

item.title: What can functional transcranial Doppler ultrasonography reveal about the cerebral lateralization of writing.
item.description:
FEBS letters
Written language is central to modern life, yet its cerebral lateralization remains far less understood than that of oral language. This review synthesizes evidence from five functional transcranial Doppler ultrasonography (fTCD) studies (n = 268; 228 adults and 40 children aged 7-9 years), a method well-suited to studying writing due to its tolerance of natural movement. The linguistic component of writing has been shown to be left-lateralized in right-handers, mirroring oral language, whereas for left-handers findings remain inconclusive. Linguistic processing appears largely independent of whether words are produced by hand or keyboard. The unresolved issue is dissociating linguistic from motor components as writing movements may themselves be intrinsically linguistic. Future research should address underexplored populations and leverage writing as a model for neuroplasticity.

item.title: Behavioral dimensions and white matter organization in early childhood following preterm birth
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Background: Children born preterm are at increased risk for attentional, social and emotional challenges, collectively referred to as the preterm behavioral phenotype. While white matter alterations have been linked to individual behavioral domains following preterm birth, it remains unclear whether distinct dimensions of behavioral variability are associated with specific patterns of white matter organization. Understanding neurobiological risk markers for preterm phenotypic traits may help identify children at greatest risk. Objective: We investigated the extent to which these behavioral traits covary across the gestational age spectrum and whether latent behavioral dimensions are associated with white matter micro- and macro-structure in young children born preterm. Methods: We collected behavioral and diffusion MRI data from 58 children born preterm (29 females; mean age = 5.64 ± 0.99 years; GA range = 24-36 weeks) and 85 full-term children aged 4-8 years (44 females; mean age = 5.91 ± 0.95 years; mean GA = 39.26 ± 1.24 weeks). Principal component analyses were performed separately in preterm, full-term, and combined groups to characterize latent behavioral dimensions spanning autism-related traits, ADHD symptoms, and emotional functioning. Fixel-based analysis was then used to examine associations between behavioral dimensions and fiber density and fiber cross-section, adjusting for demographic and perinatal factors. Results: In the preterm sample, autism- and ADHD-related behaviors emerged as relatively distinct dimensions, whereas behavioral variance in the full-term sample was captured by a broad neurodevelopmental dimension. In children born preterm, higher scores on the ADHD-related behavioral dimension were associated with reduced fiber cross-section in the splenium of the corpus callosum. No significant associations were found for fiber density in the preterm or full-term samples. Conclusions: These findings suggest that prematurity influences not only behavioral outcomes, but also how those outcomes relate to white matter organization, highlighting the importance of considering behavioral heterogeneity when investigating brain-behavior relationships in preterm populations.
